questions.stem: An application must encrypt 50 MB files with a key that is protected by AWS KMS. Which combination of steps should the developer take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Send each file to the KMS Encrypt API and store the ciphertext that it returns
options.rationale: Encrypt accepts only small amounts of data, so it cannot encrypt large files directly.

options.text: Store the encrypted data key with the file and erase the plaintext key
options.rationale: Only AWS KMS can decrypt the stored data key, so access to the file stays under the KMS key.

options.text: Export the KMS key and encrypt the files with it directly
options.rationale: KMS keys do not leave AWS KMS unencrypted.

options.text: Call GenerateDataKey and encrypt each file locally with the plaintext key
options.rationale: GenerateDataKey returns a plaintext and an encrypted copy of a data key; the plaintext copy encrypts the data outside KMS.

options.text: Store the plaintext data key next to each file so the file can be decrypted later
options.rationale: Anyone with the file could then decrypt it.

questions.explanation: Envelope encryption: a data key from GenerateDataKey encrypts large data locally, and only the KMS-encrypted copy of that key is kept with the data. Calling Encrypt directly is the trap, because it accepts only small payloads.

questions.stem: Objects in an Amazon S3 bucket must be encrypted at rest with a key whose use is controlled by a key policy and logged in AWS CloudTrail. Which encryption option meets these requirements?

options.text: Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)
options.rationale: S3 manages these keys for you, so there is no key policy to control.

options.text: Server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C)
options.rationale: With SSE-C you manage the keys yourself outside AWS KMS.

options.text: No encryption, with a bucket policy that denies public access
options.rationale: Blocking public access is not encryption at rest.

options.text: Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (SSE-KMS)
options.rationale: SSE-KMS uses a KMS key with its own policy, and each use of it is logged in CloudTrail.

questions.explanation: Choose SSE-KMS when you need control over who can use the key and an audit trail of its use.

questions.stem: A company requires that data is encrypted before it leaves the application, so that AWS never receives it in plaintext. Which approach meets this requirement?

options.text: Client-side encryption, for example with the AWS Encryption SDK
options.rationale: Data is encrypted in the application before it is sent to AWS.

options.text: Server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys
options.rationale: S3 receives the plaintext and encrypts it on arrival.

options.text: Server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys that the company manages
options.rationale: S3 still receives the plaintext before encrypting it.

options.text: HTTPS between the application and AWS
options.rationale: TLS protects data in transit but AWS decrypts it on arrival.

questions.explanation: Server-side encryption protects data at rest after AWS receives it; client-side encryption protects it before it is sent.

questions.stem: A security review requires that all requests to an Amazon S3 bucket use HTTPS. What should the developer add?

options.text: Default bucket encryption with SSE-S3 applied to every object that is uploaded
options.rationale: Default encryption protects data at rest, not in transit.

options.text: A bucket policy that denies requests where aws:SecureTransport is false
options.rationale: The condition blocks any request made over plain HTTP.

options.text: S3 Versioning
options.rationale: Versioning keeps object versions and has nothing to do with transport.

options.text: An S3 Lifecycle rule
options.rationale: Lifecycle rules move and delete objects by age.

questions.explanation: The aws:SecureTransport condition key is the standard way to require TLS for a bucket.

questions.stem: An Application Load Balancer needs a public TLS certificate for www.example.com that renews automatically. What should the developer use?

options.text: A self-signed certificate imported into ACM and attached to the listener
options.rationale: Browsers do not trust self-signed certificates, and imported ones are not renewed by ACM.

options.text: A certificate from AWS Private CA
options.rationale: Private certificates are trusted only inside your organization, not by public browsers.

options.text: A public ACM certificate attached to the HTTPS listener
options.rationale: ACM issues public certificates and manages their renewal, automatically when DNS validation is used.

options.text: An Amazon EC2 key pair
options.rationale: Key pairs are for SSH access, not TLS.

questions.explanation: The clues are a public certificate and automatic renewal, which a public ACM certificate on the listener provides. AWS Private CA is the nearest distractor, but browsers do not trust private certificates.

questions.stem: A developer requested an ACM certificate in the eu-west-1 Region, but it does not appear when configuring a custom domain for an Amazon CloudFront distribution. What should the developer do?

options.text: Add the eu-west-1 certificate's ARN to the distribution's origin settings
options.rationale: Origin settings describe where CloudFront fetches content; the viewer certificate must come from ACM in us-east-1.

options.text: Wait for the certificate to replicate to all Regions
options.rationale: ACM certificates are Regional and do not replicate.

options.text: Upload the certificate to the S3 origin bucket
options.rationale: Origins do not supply certificates for the distribution's domain.

options.text: Request or import the certificate in the US East (N. Virginia) Region
options.rationale: CloudFront uses certificates from ACM in us-east-1.

questions.explanation: Certificates for CloudFront must be in us-east-1, whatever Region the origin is in.

questions.stem: Internal microservices must use TLS certificates issued by the company's own certificate authority. The certificates do not need to be trusted by public browsers. Which service should the developer use?

options.text: AWS Private CA
options.rationale: Private CA issues private certificates for internal services and devices.

options.text: Public certificates from AWS Certificate Manager
options.rationale: Public certificates are for publicly trusted domains.

options.text: AWS Secrets Manager
options.rationale: Secrets Manager stores and rotates secrets; it does not issue certificates.

options.text: AWS KMS asymmetric keys
options.rationale: KMS keys sign and encrypt data but are not a certificate authority.

questions.explanation: Use AWS Private CA for an internal PKI; use public ACM certificates for public endpoints.

questions.stem: A developer needs an SSH key pair to connect to a new development instance. The developer wants AWS to keep only the public key. What should the developer do?

options.text: Create an asymmetric key in AWS KMS and download its private key
options.rationale: KMS never exports the private key of an asymmetric KMS key.

options.text: Create an EC2 key pair and download its private key once
options.rationale: EC2 stores the public key and gives you the private key once.

options.text: Request a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager
options.rationale: ACM certificates are for TLS, not SSH sign-in.

options.text: Store a password in AWS Secrets Manager
options.rationale: A password is not an SSH key pair.

questions.explanation: EC2 key pairs (created in EC2 or imported) are the standard way to get SSH keys for instances.

questions.stem: Application logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs sometimes contain email addresses and credit card numbers. Most people who read the logs must not see these values. What should the developer configure?

options.text: AWS KMS encryption of the log group with a customer managed key that rotates
options.rationale: Encryption protects data at rest, but anyone allowed to read the logs still sees the values.

options.text: A shorter retention period
options.rationale: Shorter retention limits how long data is kept, not who sees it.

options.text: A data protection policy on the log group that masks sensitive data
options.rationale: Matching data is masked when the logs are viewed unless the reader has unmask permission.

options.text: A metric filter that counts the sensitive values
options.rationale: Metric filters create metrics; they do not hide log content.

questions.explanation: The clue is that most readers must not see the values: a data protection policy masks them for anyone without unmask permission. Encryption is the trap, because it protects stored data but not what an allowed reader sees.

questions.stem: A Lambda function connects to an Amazon RDS database. The password must not appear in code or configuration and must rotate automatically. Which steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Package the password in a Lambda layer
options.rationale: The secret would sit in plaintext in every function that uses the layer.

options.text: Allow the execution role to read the secret, and fetch it at runtime
options.rationale: With secretsmanager:GetSecretValue, the function fetches the current password when it needs it.

options.text: Store the password as a String parameter in Parameter Store
options.rationale: A plain String parameter is not encrypted and does not rotate.

options.text: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation
options.rationale: Secrets Manager rotates database credentials on a schedule.

options.text: Store the password in an environment variable and redeploy to rotate it
options.rationale: The password is visible in the configuration and rotation is manual.

questions.explanation: Secrets Manager plus a runtime lookup keeps secrets out of code and supports rotation; caching the value reduces calls.
